newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-State cash to help German media firm Kirch.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-State cash to help German media firm Kirch.

text.p: Germany stretched out a helping hand to Leo Kirch on Monday as banks offered a massive state-sponsored loan to the Bavarian media mogul whose bid to dominate German digital pay television appears under threat.

Just weeks after British Sky Broadcasting Plc abandoned plans to invest in his DF1 digital station, Kirch is negotiating a credit line estimated at some one billion marks ($591.2 million) with a group of state-owned and commercial banks.

The news comes amid mounting signs that Kirch's digital TV plans have gone awry. His DF1 service has attracted fewer than 30,000 customers in its starting months and Kirch has been forced back into talks on a possible co-operation with rival Bertelsmann AG.
It was unclear on Monday what the precise scale of the loan being negotiated was or what the money would be used for. Kirch would only confirm that talks were taking place.

However leading creditor Landesanstalt fuer Aufbaufinanzierung (LfA), a bank controlled by the Bavarian state government, said it alone would provide Kirch with "several hundred million marks" in credit.
Industry sources named other participants in the loan as Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Commerzbank AG but neither bank was prepared to comment.
Sources also said that Kirch's DF1 network was unlikely to benefit directly from the new funds, which would likely be channeled into films.
Kirch has already run up massive bills in an eight-billion-mark shopping spree to secure blockbuster programming, including rights to the 2002 soccer World Cup.
Rival pay TV channel Premiere noted that it was "relatively unusual" for the government to step in to fund the build-up of a company.
"We have to wonder what it means for competition if the state has to help someone build up the digital TV business they failed to build up alone," a Premiere spokeswoman said.

But Premiere, Germany's only analogue pay TV channel which is controlled by Kirch arch-rival Bertelsmann AG and Canal Plus of France, said it was still negotiating a possible link-up between its customer base and the DF1 digital platform.
Weak sales have forced Kirch back into talks with Bertelsmann and Canal Plus after he parted company with them in a highly publicised squabble over decoder standards last July.
"We are still fundamentally in favour of links. Which is not to say we cannot survive without such an agreement," Premiere's spokeswoman said.

With some 1.5 million subscribers, Premiere has been able to launch its own pilot digital TV project with some 30,000 subscribers and believes thousands more would be willing to trade their analogue services for digital services.

Digital technology allows broadcasters to squeeze more channels into cable and satellite networks and show films in very high quality. It also allows new media forms such as video on demand and home-shopping.

A deal with Premiere would also ease Kirch's legal troubles. Premiere has repeatedly challenged Kirch in court and in February achieved a major victory when it blocked DF1 from advertising outside its home region of Bavaria.
Kirch still owns 25 percent of Premiere and is its main supplier of films.
Kirch is also thought to be close to a deal with Deutsche Telekom AG, which has so far refused to endorse Kirch's decoder technology.
This and other differences have kept DF1 outside Telekom's cable TV network that links 16.7 million homes and confined the channel to satellite broadcasts only.
Telekom chairman Ron Sommer said earlier this month he hoped the deadlock on talks could be broken in time for Christmas. ($ = 1.691 German Marks)
